body:
WEBVTT

1
00:00:00.600 --> 00:00:03.457
Every research project begins with a
topic,

2
00:00:03.577 --> 00:00:07.251
but a topic is not something you can
research.

3
00:00:07.371 --> 00:00:12.677
A topic is an area of interest, like
social media or climate policy.

4
00:00:12.797 --> 00:00:16.878
A question is something you can actually
answer with evidence.

5
00:00:16.998 --> 00:00:23.121
In this topic we will look at how to move
from one to the other,

6
00:00:23.241 --> 00:00:27.731
and why that move matters so much for
everything that follows.

7
00:00:28.351 --> 00:00:31.208
Think of the process as a funnel.

8
00:00:31.328 --> 00:00:34.185
At the top sits your broad topic.

9
00:00:34.305 --> 00:00:37.570
Each step down the funnel adds a
constraint.

10
00:00:37.690 --> 00:00:42.996
You might narrow by population, by place,
by time period or by outcome.

11
00:00:43.116 --> 00:00:48.831
By the bottom of the funnel you have
something small enough to study properly,

12
00:00:48.951 --> 00:00:54.257
but still connected to the area that
interested you in the first place.

13
00:00:54.877 --> 00:00:57.734
The first constraint is usually the
population.

14
00:00:57.854 --> 00:01:01.119
Social media is too broad, but social
media

15
00:01:01.239 --> 00:01:04.913
use among first year nursing students is
much narrower.

16
00:01:05.033 --> 00:01:11.155
If you cannot describe your population in
a sentence, the question is not ready yet.

17
00:01:11.775 --> 00:01:17.081
A useful tool for health and social care
questions is the PICO framework.

18
00:01:17.201 --> 00:01:20.875
Peek oh stands for population,
intervention, comparison and outcome.

19
00:01:20.995 --> 00:01:24.260
Filling in each part forces you to be

20
00:01:24.380 --> 00:01:28.053
explicit about what you are measuring and
against what.

21
00:01:28.173 --> 00:01:31.031
Not every question needs all four parts,

22
00:01:31.151 --> 00:01:36.865
but working through them quickly shows
which parts of your question are still vague.

23
00:01:37.485 --> 00:01:41.975
Once you know your outcome, decide how you
would measure it.

24
00:01:42.095 --> 00:01:46.176
You might use a like it scale in a
questionnaire,

25
00:01:46.296 --> 00:01:49.153
a set of interviews, or existing records.

26
00:01:49.273 --> 00:01:53.355
If you cannot imagine any way to measure
the outcome,

27
00:01:53.475 --> 00:01:57.149
that is a sign the question needs more
work.

28
00:01:57.269 --> 00:02:02.575
The measurement you choose will also shape
the design of the whole study.

29
00:02:03.195 --> 00:02:06.868
Before you commit, check your question
against three tests.

30
00:02:06.988 --> 00:02:10.662
Is it answerable with evidence you could
realistically collect?

31
00:02:10.782 --> 00:02:16.088
Is it narrow enough that you can actually
get it done in time?

32
00:02:16.208 --> 00:02:18.657
And does it still interest you?

33
00:02:18.777 --> 00:02:21.634
A good research question passes all three,

34
00:02:21.754 --> 00:02:26.244
and it will guide every decision you make
from here on.

35
00:02:26.364 --> 00:02:29.629
Write it down, share it with a colleague,

36
00:02:29.749 --> 00:02:35.055
and ask them to explain it back to you in
their own words.
